2026-12-26.title: Saint Stephen, the First Martyr · Feast
readings: Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit
It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father
2026-12-26.alt: Feast, within the Octave of Christmas. Liturgical colour: red.
2026-12-26.verse: While they were stoning Stephen, he prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then he knelt down and cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”
theo: The day after Christmas the Church wears red. It can seem a sudden change, from the crib to the stones. But the Fathers saw the connection: “Yesterday Christ was born on earth so that today Stephen might be born in heaven” (St Fulgentius). The Child came to give his life; those who follow him may be asked to give theirs. Christmas is not sentimental; it is the beginning of a love that goes to the Cross.

Stephen, “full of grace and power”, was one of the seven deacons chosen to serve the poor (Acts 6:1–6). He also preached with wisdom no one could withstand, as Jesus had promised (Matthew 10:19–20). Accused before the council, he saw “the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God”. As he was stoned he prayed two prayers that echo Jesus' own on the Cross: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” and “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” The martyr is the perfect disciple: he dies like his Master.

Standing nearby, holding the coats of the stoners, was a young man named Saul (Acts 7:58). St Augustine said: “If Stephen had not prayed, the Church would not have had Paul.” Forgiveness is never wasted; it bears fruit we may never see.
conn: Stephen is called the Protomartyr, the first to die for Christ after Pentecost. His name means “crown” in Greek.
Compare Luke 23:46 (“Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”) and Luke 23:34 (“Father, forgive them”). Luke wrote both his Gospel and Acts and deliberately shows Stephen dying like Jesus.
Elsewhere Christ is seated at God's right hand. Here he stands, as if rising to welcome his witness or to plead his cause.

Stephen was among the first seven deacons, ordained to serve at tables so that the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the word (Acts 6:2–6). Service of the poor and witness to the truth belong together.
Acts 7:58 introduces Saul, the future St Paul, holding the cloaks. Stephen's forgiving prayer is followed, two chapters later, by Saul's conversion.
The carol “Good King Wenceslas” is set on the Feast of Stephen, when the king goes out in the snow to bring food to a poor man.
altar: In the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I), after the consecration, Stephen is the first name in the list of saints: “John the Baptist, Stephen, Matthias, Barnabas…”
The Eucharist gives the strength of the martyrs. The same Christ who strengthened Stephen comes to us under the form of bread to make us faithful witnesses.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, yesterday we sang carols around the crib. Today the priest wears red, and we hear about stones and death. Why?

An ancient bishop, St Fulgentius, explained: “Yesterday Christ was born on earth so that today Stephen might be born in heaven.” The Child of Bethlehem came to give his life. Christmas is the beginning of a love that will go all the way to the Cross, and those who follow him are invited into that same love.

Stephen was a deacon, chosen to serve the poor widows at table. He was also full of the Holy Spirit and spoke with such wisdom that no one could answer him. When they dragged him out to stone him, he looked up and saw heaven open and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.

And listen to his last words: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” And: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” These are almost exactly the words of Jesus on the Cross. Stephen died the way Jesus died, forgiving.

Standing there, holding the coats of those who threw the stones, was a young man named Saul. He later became St Paul, the great apostle. St Augustine said: “If Stephen had not prayed, the Church would not have had Paul.” Forgiveness is never wasted.

So this Christmas, let us ask: is there someone I need to forgive? A family member, a neighbour, a colleague? Let us pray for them by name, as Stephen did. And let us remember the Christians who suffer for their faith today. The joy of Christmas is strong enough to face even this.
kids: Children, today is the feast of St Stephen. He loved Jesus very much.
He helped poor people and told everyone about Jesus. Some people got angry and threw stones at him.
But Stephen did something amazing: he forgave them, just like Jesus did on the Cross.
Is there someone you need to forgive? Say: “Jesus, help me forgive.”

intro: Before he was a martyr, Stephen was a deacon chosen to serve the widows (Acts 6:1–6).

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, yesterday we celebrated the birth of Christ; today we celebrate the birth into heaven of the first martyr. But before Stephen was a martyr, he was a deacon who served at tables.

In the early Church in Jerusalem there was a complaint: the widows of the Greek-speaking Christians were being neglected in the daily distribution of food. The apostles asked the community to choose seven men of good standing, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, to take care of this service. Stephen was the first named (Acts 6:1–6). His holiness began in a very practical task: making sure poor widows got their food.

Luke tells us that Stephen, full of grace and power, did great wonders and signs among the people, and that his opponents could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke (Acts 6:8–10). When he stood before the Council, his face was like the face of an angel (Acts 6:15). The man who served tables became a fearless witness. Faithfulness in small things prepared him for great things.

And when the stones began to fly, Stephen prayed with the words of his Master: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit; and kneeling down he cried out: Lord, do not hold this sin against them (Acts 7:59–60). He died as Jesus had died, entrusting himself to God and forgiving his killers. Among the witnesses was a young man named Saul, who would become the apostle Paul. Stephen's forgiveness bore fruit.

So Stephen gives us a Christmas programme: serve humbly, witness boldly, forgive completely. Is there someone in your family you have not forgiven? This is the season to let go. The Child in the manger came to make forgiveness possible. Let us ask St Stephen to help us live what we receive at this Holy Mass.

opts.a: Teaching homily: martyrdom and Christian witness
intro: Martyr means witness. Today let us understand why the Church honours martyrs so highly.

sub: A witness to the truth of faith, to the point of death (CCC 2473).
Bound to Christ by charity.
Not suicide, not violence; freely accepting death rather than denying Christ.
points.apply: Thank God for the martyrs of our own land.

points.h: The blood of martyrs is seed
sub: Tertullian's saying.
Persecution has never destroyed the Church.
Christians still die for their faith today.
Most of us are called to white martyrdom: daily fidelity.
Courage to speak and to act as Christians.
Gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15–16).
points.apply: Do not hide your faith at work or school this week.

concl: Martyrdom is the supreme witness, and every Christian is called to bear witness.
The Church today is still a Church of martyrs.
opts.resolve: This week I will pray for persecuted Christians and not hide my faith.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the word martyr comes from the Greek word for witness. The Catechism says that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: it means bearing witness even unto death; the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity (CCC 2473).

A martyr is not someone who seeks death or uses violence. The martyrs of the Church never killed anyone. They freely accepted death rather than deny Christ, and they died forgiving. Stephen is the first of a long line: the apostles, the martyrs of the Roman persecutions, the martyrs of Japan, Uganda, Vietnam, Mexico, and in our own land the martyr Devasahayam and many others.

In the second century Tertullian wrote that the blood of martyrs is the seed of Christians. After Stephen's death a severe persecution broke out and the believers were scattered, but those who were scattered went from place to place proclaiming the word (Acts 8:1–4). Persecution has never destroyed the Church; it has spread it. And today, more Christians suffer for their faith than at any time in history. Let us pray for them often.

Most of us will not be asked to shed our blood. But all of us are called to witness. The Fathers spoke of white martyrdom: the daily dying to self, fidelity in marriage and vocation, honesty when dishonesty would be easier, refusing to join in mockery of the faith. St Peter tells us always to be ready to give an account of the hope that is in us, yet with gentleness and reverence (1 Peter 3:15–16).

So on this second day of Christmas, let us thank God for the martyrs, pray for persecuted Christians, and ask for courage. The Child of Bethlehem was born to die for us; Stephen died for Him. At this Holy Mass let us ask for the grace to live for Him.

intro: Theme: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”
Stephen, deacon and first martyr, dies like his Master, forgiving.

sub: A deacon who served the poor.

Christ speaks through his witnesses.
q: Now go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you are to speak.

When they hand you over, do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say; for what you are to say will be given to you at that time; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.

sub: Stephen looks up.
He sees Jesus standing.
The martyr's eyes are fixed on Christ.
q: Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God.

But filled with the Holy Spirit, he gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. “Look,” he said, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”
points.apply: Pray “Into your hands I commend my spirit” tonight.

sub: The Servant intercedes for transgressors.

q: Therefore I will allot him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he poured out himself to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

While they were stoning Stephen, he prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then he knelt down and cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he died.
